item.title: Perseverance Update: The Ghostly Rocks of ‘Idubi’ — Bright Remnants of Aqueous Systems from Long Ago
item.description: Explore This Section Perseverance Home Mission Overview Rover Components Mars Rock Samples Where is Perseverance? Ingenuity Mars Helicopter Mission Updates Science Overview Objectives Instruments Highlights Exploration Goals News and Features Multimedia Perseverance Raw Images Images Videos Audio More Resources Mars Missions Mars Perseverance Rover Mars Curiosity Rover Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter Mars Odyssey More Mars Missions Mars Home 2 min read Perseverance Update: The Ghostly Rocks of ‘Idubi’ — Bright Remnants of Aqueous Systems from Long Ago NASA’s Perseverance rover captured this image of a bright, silica-rich rock in the “Idubi” area using its left Mastcam-Z camera on Oct. 29, 2026 (Sol 2023) at the local mean solar time of 13:03:53. NASA/JPL-Caltech/ASU Written by Candice Bedford, Research Scientist at Purdue University Date: Nov. 16, 2026 During the Perseverance rover’s investigation of “Idubi” — an area of ancient Martian crust exposed in the “Lac de Charmes” region, outside of Jezero crater — the Perseverance rover team has been captivated by a cluster of eerily bright, light-toned rocks in the area. These bright fragments stand out sharply against the underlying darker and often dust-covered Martian surface, and are even brighter than the igneous and impactite rocks we previously investigated. Suspecting that they differed from the typical igneous rocks in the area, the rover team directed Perseverance to investigate. Newly downlinked data from the SuperCam instrument has confirmed that these light-toned rocks are not igneous in origin and instead are rich in hydrated silica. Hydrated silica can form in many aqueous environments on the Earth, including hydrothermal, pedogenic, and groundwater systems. As such, these types of deposits are prime targets for understanding Mars’ hydrological history, as several of these environments could have been capable of supporting life. Furthermore, hydrated silica holds immense astrobiological value due to its remarkable capacity to preserve microfossils. Could these pale remnants of an ancient Martian water system hold signs of ancient life? When Perseverance previously encountered silica-rich rocks on the inner rim of Jezero Crater, the deposits were too small to deploy proximity science instruments and gather the high-resolution chemical and mineralogical data needed to constrain their origin and biosignature preservation potential. Fortunately, the rocks at “Idubi” offer a much more promising scale, and a detailed proximity science campaign is already underway. item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 16, 1974: The giant Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico broadcasts humanity's 1st interstellar message
item.description: null On Nov. 16, 1974, humans sent their first message to the stars in an attempt to contact extraterrestrials. They did this using what was then the largest radio telescope in the world, located at the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico. A group of scientists led by Frank Drake and Carl Sagan sent their message to the M13 star cluster . The message was written in binary code and contained information about human DNA. It also included figures of a human, the solar system and the Arecibo telescope. The idea was that if any aliens were to receive the signal and figure out how to decode it, they would know where it came from. Because M13 is 25,000 light-years away, it will take 25,000 years for any M13 aliens to hear our message — if they are even out there. (Image credit: SETI) Why it mattered The Arecibo message is only one of several messages intended for extraterrestrials, but this signal sent from Puerto Rico in 1974 was humanity's first intentional olive branch to the stars. At the time, it was the most powerful broadcast ever beamed into space, according to the SETI Institute. "The broadcast was particularly powerful because it used Arecibo's megawatt transmitter attached to its 305 meter antenna," SETI wrote of the broadcast in a project over. "The emission was equivalent to a 20 trillion watt omnidirectional broadcast, and would be detectable by a SETI experiment just about anywhere in the galaxy, assuming a receiving antenna similar in size to Arecibo's." The message was designed by astronomy professor Frank Drake of Cornell University (who also developed the famed Drake Equation for alien life), as well as Cornnell graduate students Richard Isaacman and Linda May, and Arecibo staff member James Walker, with input from astronomer Carl Sagan and others, according to Cornell University . The message included 1,679 bits that were arranged in 73 lines of 23 characters per line, all prime numbers, with the broadcast lasting less than 3 minutes, according to SETI. As of 2026, the message should have traveled about 52 light-years (1 light-year is the distance light travels in a year), with 24,948 light-years to go before reaching star cluster M13. The Arecibo message may have been the first message of its kind, but it wasn't the last. We have also included messages on several spacecraft, such as Pioneer and Voyager. NASA and Paul McCartney also b eamed a performance of "Across the Universe" in 2008. Want more space history? item.title: Relive Starship’s historic Flight 15 with our best photos from launch and ‘Mechazilla’ tower catch
item.description: null STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX has officially wrapped up the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket, successfully catching the vehicle's upper stage for the first time. Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility here in South Texas on Friday (Nov. 13). The mission was billed as the first to bring both of Starship's stages, the Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage, back to the launch site for recovery. And, while SpaceX was forced to divert Super Heavy's return to an off-shore splashdown (and explosion), the upper stage managed to survive its 22-hour jaunt in orbit and plunge through the atmosphere for a picture-perfect catch by the launch tower back at Starbase. It was the first-ever Ship catch, and a huge milestone toward SpaceX's ultimate goal: making Starship completely reusable. Liftoff occurred from Pad 2 at 5:47 p.m. EST (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local time) on Friday, against a near cloudless blue sky. Super Heavy is powered by 33 Raptor 3 engines, which provide more than 18 million pounds of thrust at liftoff. And lift off the booster did. The 33 Raptor engines of SpaceX's Starship V3 rocket during its test flight from Starbase, Texas on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner) Starship roared off the pad under the power of those Raptors, pulsing visible shockwaves through the plume ejected from the rocket's flame trench. Starship climbs the sky above Starbase, Texas on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner) The first couple minutes of flight went nominally; the vehicle climbed into the sky, gearing up for the hot-staging separation of Super Heavy and Ship — all of which was visible for miles, thanks to the clear Texas skies. Space.com's images taken from the media’s launch viewing area were shot on a Canon R5 Mark II , with an RF 200-800mm lens that made the sharp pictures of Starship’s liftoff and return possible from almost 4 miles away. item.title: NASA Receives 16th Consecutive ‘Clean’ Financial Audit Opinion
item.description: Credit: NASA For the 16th consecutive year, NASA has received an unmodified, or “clean,” opinion from an external auditor on its fiscal year 2026 financial statements. The rating is the best possible audit opinion, certifying that NASA’s financial statements conform with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles for federal agencies and accurately present the agency’s financial position. “Our responsibility at NASA is to be disciplined stewards of the resources entrusted to us by the American people while delivering on the missions they expect from this agency,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Our 16th consecutive clean audit reflects a long record of financial accountability, and we intend to pair that discipline with the urgency and execution required to take on the near-impossible missions ahead.” The 2026 Agency Financial Report provides key financial and performance information and demonstrates the agency’s commitment to transparency in the use of American taxpayers’ dollars. In addition, the 2026 report presents progress during the past year, and spotlights advancements in NASA missions, objectives, and workforce development with these financial resources. In fiscal year 2026 (FY 2026), NASA’s 10-day Artemis II mission successfully accomplished a test flight around the Moon with four crew members, delivering major human spaceflight milestones, such as the record‑breaking distance astronauts have traveled from Earth and global public engagement. NASA also announced a series of transformative agencywide initiatives designed to advance American leadership in space, including plans to build a Moon Base, which will be humanity’s first lunar outpost, and a place where astronauts will live, work, and explore near the Moon’s South Pole. NASA’s science advancements in FY 2026 included launching the agency’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, ahead of schedule, to study dark matter, dark energy, planets outside our solar system, as well as exploration of everything from nearby stars to distant galaxies. NASA’s experimental X-59 quiet supersonic aircraft achieved a major milestone when it flew faster than the speed of sound for the first time. The agency also: launched NASA Force with the U.S. Office of Personnel Management, a talent track designed to recruit and deploy the nation’s top engineers and technologists to support America’s space program; announced an agencywide realignment to increase mission focus; and welcomed additional Artemis Accords signatories committing to the safe, transparent, and responsible exploration of the Moon, Mars, and beyond. item.title: Elon Musk says SpaceX’s Starship, already the largest rocket on Earth, will get even bigger with next-gen V4 model
item.description: null As usual, SpaceX and its founder Elon Musk are thinking big. The company recovered the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever on Saturday (Nov. 14), plucking it out of the sky with the "chopstick" arms of its Texas launch tower. It was a huge moment for SpaceX , bringing its vision of full and rapid rocket reuse much closer to reality. But Elon Musk isn't one to dwell on the past or rest on laurels, so he soon outlined an even more ambitious future for Starship. "Starship V4 will be ~70m [230 feet] long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load," Musk said via X, the social media platform he owns, on Sunday evening (Nov. 15). "Engine count will be raised to 9, with 3 more Raptor-Vacuum engines added, and these will be higher-thrust V4 engines." The current version of Starship — the one that launched Friday (Nov. 13) on the vehicle's 15th test flight — is the V3. It's the largest and most powerful rocket ever built, standing 408 feet (124 m) tall when fully stacked with its Super Heavy first stage and Ship upper stage. V3's Ship is 171 feet (52 m) tall and features six of SpaceX's Raptor V3 engines. (The similarly reusable Super Heavy V3 booster is powered by 33 Raptors.) So, as Musk noted in his post, the V4 Ship will be quite an upgrade in size and power. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk shared this chart depicting the evolution of SpaceX's Starship vehicles from the V2 to the planned V4 variant in August 2025. Exact specifications for Starship V4 are evolving. (Image credit: SpaceX/Elon Musk) Starship Die Cast Rocket Model Was $47.99 Now $39.99 on Amazon . Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g. View Deal To provide a little perspective about that vehicle's planned dimensions: The V4 Ship will be the same height as a fully stacked Falcon 9 , SpaceX's workhorse two-stage rocket, and much broader: Ship is 30 feet (9 m) across, while the Falcon 9's payload fairing is 17.1 feet (5.2 m) wide. This isn't the first we've heard about a V4 Starship. Back in August 2025, for example, Musk posted a graphic showing Starship's planned progression from the V2 to the V3 to the V4, which he said is expected to debut in 2027. That slide pegs the future Starship's total height at 466 feet (142 m), 200 feet (61 m) of which would be Ship. But those numbers are out of date, Musk stressed in the post, saying that V4 is "probably closer to 150m height." So, yeah: If all goes according to plan, the next Starship will be nearly 500 feet tall. item.title: What exactly is a light-day? Here's what Voyager 1's latest milestone means for the interstellar probe
item.description: null After nearly 50 years traveling through space, NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is approaching a milestone no human-made object has reached before: a distance of one light-day from Earth. This milestone — which Voyager 1 is expected to reach on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (1016:07 GMT) — highlights the immense distances Voyager 1 has traveled and the challenges of communicating with spacecraft operating in the outer reaches of the solar system and beyond. Astronomers use a measurement known as a light-day to describe how far light travels in 24 hours. Light moves at approximately 186,000 miles (300,000 kilometers) per second, meaning one light-day is roughly 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), according to a statement from NASA. Although the term light-day might sound like a measurement of time, it is actually a unit of distance, much like a light-year . Astronomers use light-based measurements because conventional miles and kilometers become increasingly difficult to comprehend when describing the enormous distances between objects in space. For perspective on how far Voyager 1 has travelled, sunlight takes about eight minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth, meaning our planet is approximately 8.3 light-minutes from the sun. Radio signals traveling between Earth and Mars can take anywhere from three to 22 minutes, depending on the planets' positions in their orbits, according to the statement. By comparison, when Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth , a radio signal sent from the probe will take a full 24 hours to reach mission controllers on Earth, and a command transmitted from Earth will take another 24 hours to reach the spacecraft. A NASA visualization showing Voyager 1 looking back towards the solar system as it approaches one light-day away from Earth. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) The communication delay affects how engineers operate spacecraft at such distances. Unlike spacecraft operating closer to Earth, which can receive commands and return data with relatively little delay, communicating with Voyager 1 requires mission controllers to account for the extended signal travel time when planning spacecraft operations, troubleshooting technical issues and evaluating the results of commands sent to the probe. Voyager 1 has been traveling away from Earth since its launch on Sept. 5, 1977 . Now cruising through interstellar space at nearly 38,000 mph (61,000 kph), the spacecraft has spent more than 49 years covering the distance that light can cross in a single day. Even at that speed, Voyager 1 is moving relatively slowly compared with light itself. Its twin, Voyager 2 , which launched in 1977 on a different trajectory, is expected to reach the same one-light-day milestone in November 2035. item.title: 'Maybe the scariest thing I've heard in my life': Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover reveals his toughest challenge before flying to the moon
item.description: null TENERIFE, Canary Islands — Former NASA astronaut Victor Glover has flown in combat, performed four spacewalks and strapped himself to the top of rockets launching into space. But before embarking on his historic Artemis II journey around the moon, he faced something even more difficult: a conversation with his four daughters. Speaking alongside former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival in Tenerife, Canary Islands, on Oct. 18, Glover opened up about the challenges of preparing his family for his riskiest mission yet. "This is maybe the greatest challenge of my astronaut career," Glover said. Glover joined NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman and Christina Koch and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen aboard NASA's Artemis II mission, which launched on April 1 , 2026, marking humanity's first crewed journey to the moon since Apollo 17 in 1972. But preparing for the historic journey wasn't just about mastering the spacecraft and executing the mission successfully. It also meant making sure his family was ready for what lay ahead. When Glover first traveled to space aboard SpaceX's Crew-1 mission in 2020, his children were much younger and he and his wife, Dionna, made a conscious effort to prepare them for his time in space. "We decided, as a parental unit, Dionna and I, that we were going to put as much effort into making sure our family was ready as NASA was putting into making sure I was ready to be a crew member," Glover explained. Victor Glover speaking at the Starmus VIII festival in Tenerife, Canary Islands, on Oct. 18, 2026. (Image credit: Daisy Dobrijevic/Future) The family visited NASA's Kennedy Space Center , toured the launch pad and crew quarters and even planned when Glover would call home from the International Space Station . But by the time Artemis II came around, things were different. All four of his daughters were now adults, and preparing them for his journey around the moon meant discussing the mission's risks, including the possibility that he might not return home. Glover recalled his wife telling him something he described as maybe the scariest thing he'd ever heard. "You should have this talk with our daughters." And although he knew she was right, it wasn't an easy conversation to have. "We did, and it did not go well in my opinion," Glover admitted. "Well, it's not about going well. The talk needed to be done, just because it's hard." The following day, Glover sent his daughters and wife a poem, Live Your Life , by Chief Tecumseh. The poem helped Glover express something he had struggled to put into words during their conversation: why he believed the risks of traveling to the moon were worth taking. "It was a very tough conversation, but they understood that I know this is risky. I wasn't just telling them Dad's risking his life. item.title: How I used evidence and imagination to write an account of the world in 2096
item.description: Fatih Aktas/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images How do you invent the future? This isn’t a question that I had ever had to consider until I set out to imagine what the world would be like in 70 years’ time for New Scientist ’s 70th anniversary. As a lifelong sci-fi nerd, I have read and watched loads of material that could have served as inspiration. But this being New Scientist , I wanted to make sure that I was as grounded in real science and technology as possible – while acknowledging that no prediction of the future is ever correct. I began by asking my colleagues on the magazine for their ideas about the future and then attempted to corral this sci-fi smorgasbord into something resembling an outline of a self-consistent narrative. Part of the problem in imagining many different futures is that they contradict themselves – you can’t have the war-torn AI dystopia of Terminator alongside the utopia of Star Trek . I wanted both hope and realism in my future, so I decided to look at how the scientific literature handles the end of the century. One of the most obvious forecasts is for climate change, where we have a pretty good idea about what might happen in 2096, under a range of scenarios, because it all boils down to atmospheric physics that we can model. Of course, which of these scenarios we end up with is all too dependent on human politics, so the science alone couldn’t guide me. I also turned to population projections , which, for the most part, are locked in based on current population trends. The idea that the end of the century will be the first time we are living in a world of falling populations became a fascinating strand in the final piece. Advertisement The biggest problem I faced was how to deal with AI. I am not confident making predictions on this topic even just a few years in advance – as I’ve written previously, my views on AI have evolved between the release of ChatGPT in 2022 and now , so how could I possibly predict what would happen by the time we got to 2096? Furthermore, there was a risk that AI could come to dominate the piece, crowding out everything else. There is a graph I often think about, published by the Financial Times under the headline “AI could end scarcity, end humanity – or boost [GDP] growth by 0.2 percentage points”. I knew that, to preserve any meaningful narrative, I had to restrict AI to this boring middle option, so I invented an AI-fuelled financial crisis that would see us place limits on the technology. I have no idea if such an event is likely to happen, but it seems to me to be the only way to preserve a future that remains comprehensible to us today. item.title: The Leonid meteor shower peaks Nov. 17-18! Here's what you need to know
item.description: null The Leonid meteor shower peaks Nov. 17-18 sending shooting stars and fireballs across the autumn sky as Earth passes through a stream of debris left by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. Up to 15 meteors could be spotted per hour under perfect dark sky conditions on the night of Nov. 17-18, according to the International Meteor Organisation . NASA, meanwhile, has given a more conservative rate of less than three meteors per hour — time will tell. Leonid meteors appear to race away from a point of origin, or radiant, in the constellation Leo, which glistens high above the southeastern horizon in the hours before dawn in mid-November. Both Jupiter and Mars will be separated by just a few degrees in the constellation Leo on the night of the peak, making it particularly easy to find in 2026! When is the best time to look for Leonid meteors? The best time to spot Leonids is in the hours before dawn on Nov. 18, when the radiant will reach its highest point in the southeastern sky, maximizing the amount of meteors that may be seen skimming through Earth's atmosphere . By then, the waxing moon will have set, leaving darker skies and a better chance of spotting fainter meteors. Shooting stars that appear close to the radiant will strike Earth almost head-on, leaving the shortest trails. Instead, find a patch of sky a short distance away from the constellation Leo, where the meteors will be at their most impressive, and give your eyes 20-30 minutes to fully adapt to the dark. Why are the Leonids special? As if shooting stars weren't enough, the Leonid shower is also known for spawning dazzling fireballs and long-lasting Earth-grazing meteors , which strike our atmosphere at an oblique angle, leaving long trains as they skim through before passing back out into space. The shower is also capable of producing magnificent meteor storms when Earth passes through particularly dense trails of debris left behind by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years. Sadly, we'll have to wait a bit for the next big show. According to the Planetary Society , another Leonid meteor storm could occur as early as 2031, while a study released in August 2026 predicts potentially spectacular displays in 2033 and 2034. item.title: Massive data centres collectively use as much electricity as an entire US state
item.description: Construction work on an AI data centre in Texas covering nearly 40 square kilometres, which will have a capacity of 600 megawatts Backyard Productions/Alamy The largest data centres in the US are using roughly the same amount of power collectively each year as one of the country’s major states, according to new figures that underscore the size and impact these massive facilities are having on local power grids. The rapid development of artificial intelligence systems has triggered a “fast and furious” expansion of data centres across the US, in particular of very large “hyperscale” data centres that support AI tools, cloud computing and large language models, says Francesca Dominici at Harvard University. But tracking the power consumption and carbon emissions impact of these facilities is difficult, as many data centre operators don’t publicly report such information. Advertisement Read more SpaceXAI data centre may have led to Mississippi air pollution spike Together with colleagues, Dominici spent two years pulling together information on 403 hyperscale data centres in the US to estimate their electricity consumption and associated carbon dioxide emissions. “Doing these measurements took an enormous amount of work,” she says. The team estimates that the hyperscale data centres collectively used about 82 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity between May 2024 and April 2025, equivalent to about 1.8 per cent of total US electricity use. This electricity use outstrips the annual power consumption of states such as Missouri, Kentucky and New Jersey. The upper bound of the team’s estimate – 99 TWh per year – would see hyperscale data centres rival the annual power consumption of states such as Indiana, Michigan and Washington. This vast power consumption has a significant climate impact. The researchers estimate that roughly 54 per cent of attributed generation was supplied by fossil fuel sources, with annual carbon dioxide emissions reaching 25.7 million tonnes – equivalent to the emissions from 67 natural gas power plants . The findings are in line with international estimates of data centre power use from the International Energy Agency and are therefore “not particularly shocking”, says Alex de Vries-Gao , a data scientist at the Free University of Amsterdam. “This just confirms the magnitude of the impacts that these facilities are having across the board.” Free newsletter Sign up to The Earth Edition Sign up to newsletter But he points out that the study relies on commercial data that is difficult to independently verify, and a set of assumptions on the power use and operating capacity of each facility. “You can’t really validate the results,” he warns. In the final days of 1998, as astronauts aboard NASA's Space Shuttle Endeavor were working during one of the early missions to assemble the International Space Station , crew members from the STS-88 mission captured photographs of a dark colored, unusually shaped object drifting through space. Despite its unusual appearance in the photographs, the object had a conventional explanation, and one that was known to the astronauts at that time: it was one of several thermal covers that had been wrapped around trunnion pins used in the space station's construction. Upon noticing the "escape" of one of the covers, Mission Commander Bob Cabana remarked over the radio to fellow astronaut Jerry Ross that "one of the thermal covers got away from you." Seeing the cover drifting away, a frustrated Ross snapped a photograph of it. Yet despite the innocuous story behind the images, they have nonetheless helped fuel belief in an unusual Space Age conspiracy theory: one involving the alleged presence of an ancient satellite, presumably of alien origin, that has long been orbiting our planet — perhaps since the end of the last Ice Age. According to proponents of this theory, the object photographed by Ross in 1998 is actually what many call the " Black Knight Satellite ," and is only one piece of evidence they point to in a long succession of unrelated — and often misinterpreted — events in modern history that supposedly lend further evidence to the alleged alien spacecraft's existence. So how did such a legend gain traction in the first place, with some versions alleging that NASA and the U.S. government have worked to conceal evidence of the alleged space object's existence from the public? Odd detections at Colorado Springs Depending on which version of the story you come across, the strange roots of the Black Knight conspiracy theory might be traced all the way back to the nineteenth century, when the famous inventor Nikola Tesla began detecting unusual electrical signal s while conducting radio experiments at his laboratory in Colorado Springs. At the time, Tesla considered whether the signals might be communications from intelligent aliens on nearby planets, although the likely source had actually been terrestrial radio interference. Notably, Tesla also never claimed that the emissions might be coming from an object in Earth's orbit; nonetheless, some proponents of the Black Knight Satellite theories have incorporated Tesla's experiments into the mythos, suggesting they may represent some of the earliest detections of a mysterious object lurking near Earth. item.description: 3 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Jim Mirandy, quality assurance specialist at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, poses for a photograph at the High Pressure Gas Facility on Nov. 10, 2026. Mirandy is now a NASA civil servant at Stennis as part of the administrator’s directive to strengthen technical core competencies within the civil service workforce. NASA/Danny Nowlin The rumble of a rocket engine might be considered a soundtrack for Jim Mirandy’s life. Mirandy has grown up with NASA as a constant presence, and his path to becoming a civil servant at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, has been decades in the making. Hired under the agency’s workforce directive to restore core competencies by converting contractors to civil service, Mirandy is now a quality assurance specialist after 30 years of working as a contractor supporting NASA. “Discovery is an important job, and it is exciting to be a part of that process,” said Mirandy. “As a nation, we lead the world in space exploration, and we make that dream of reaching for the stars a reality.” His work at the nation’s largest rocket propulsion test site directly supports the agency’s mission to return American astronauts to the Moon through the Artemis program and ensure American leadership in space. By retaining Mirandy’s facility-specific expertise as a civil servant, NASA ensures that the critical propulsion testing at NASA Stennis continues to be executed with safety and quality in mind. Mirandy describes his team as an integral part of the process that provides a second set of eyes with a focus on potential hazards. As a quality assurance specialist, he serves as the agency’s close call investigator at the center, helps lead the Voluntary Protection Program, and participates in the Striving to Achieve Real Safety committee, an employee safety committee that works to keep the site safe. Mirandy also has a long resume of critical institutional contributions, including creating high pressure and cryogenic training classes that he taught for 10 years, and helping establish safety protocols throughout various locations at the center. Mirandy’s connection to America’s space agency began in childhood living in Titusville, Florida. His father, Wes Mirandy, worked for Rocketdyne at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, and Mirandy’s nearby elementary school regularly gathered to watch launches. Later, his father worked as the A-1 test stand manager for space shuttle main engine testing at NASA Stennis. “My father was by far my greatest mentor,” said Mirandy. “My dad always included us whenever he worked on something around the house, so we picked up a knack for examining problems and fixing things. item.title: Euclid space telescope discovers its 1st comet | Space photo of the day for Nov. 16, 2026
item.description: null The comet C/2026 S1 (Euclid) discovered by the Euclid mission. (Image credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, M. Pöntinen et al. 2026) The Euclid space telescope has discovered its first comet, called comet C/2026 S1, or comet Euclid for short. What is it? (Image credit: ESA/Euclid) The Euclid mission, a European Space Agency mission that launched in 2023 with contributions from NASA, spotted this previously undetected comet approximately 807 million miles (1.3 billion kilometers) away in observations captured between Sept. 16 and 24. "I was excited to see my software flag a 'streak' smeared across several images – the result of a fast-moving object. By predicting its position I could identify it in other images, in total finding it in five image sets. Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas," Mikko Pöntinen, a scientist at the University of Helsinki who made the initial discovery with a Solar System Objects Science Working Group within the Euclid Consortium, said in a statement . Following these observations, the team diligently checked current records of comets to ensure that this was, in fact, something new to us. An close up view of comet C/2026 S1 (Euclid). (Image credit: ESA/Euclid) Why is it incredible? Euclid is a mission designed to capture long, slow observations of deep space and distant galaxies and collect data to help scientists better unravel the mysteries of dark energy and dark matter. It was in not explicitly designed in any way to capture imagery of fast-moving comet hurtling through our solar system. But still, the space telescoped managed to catch this comet whirling between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn. This finding shows that Euclid can be used for more than it was intended, and that in the future scientists could use it to intentionally target other comets in the far reaches of our solar neighborhood. These kinds of observations can also help researchers to identify "noise" like comet trails in Euclid's field of view.

item.title: Dream Chaser space plane gets landing approval for debut mission in 2027
item.description: null The Dream Chaser space plane just cleared a major hurdle ahead of its planned spring 2027 spaceflight debut. Dream Chaser just received U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) approval for its return to Earth on that robotic mission, either at the space shuttle landing facility at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida or at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. "Thank you to the FAA for its collaboration and support of commercial space innovation," representatives of Sierra Space, the Colorado company that builds Dream Chaser, wrote on X on Monday (Nov. 9). The FAA's environmental assessment found that Dream Chaser "would not significantly impact the quality of the human environment" under the National Environmental Policy Act, the agency stated . (It should also be noted that the U.S. has lately been suggesting that environmental laws should be bypassed to meet quickly rising demand for launches and landings.) For example, for a potential return at Vandenberg, "sonic booms are anticipated but would be temporary, short in duration, and limited to 1.1 PSF [pounds per square foot] or less, which is similar to a thunderclap," the FAA stated. The 30-foot-long (9 meters) Dream Chaser has been in development for more than two decades. It has yet to launch to space, though it has completed a couple of drop tests from the air. Dream Chaser was an entrant in NASA's Commercial Crew series of contracts to ferry astronauts to and from the International Space Station (ISS), but it didn't end up making the cut; in 2014, NASA picked Boeing's Starliner and SpaceX's Crew Dragon to provide this taxi service. The following year, Sierra Nevada Corporation — then the entity in charge of Dream Chaser — unveiled a cargo version of the space plane. In 2016, NASA selected the company to conduct at least six uncrewed cargo flights to the ISS, but development delays repeatedly pushed those missions into the future. Dream Chaser was originally expected to fly those robotic resupply missions on United Launch Alliance's workhorse Atlas V rocket. A few years ago, however, the space plane switched over to Vulcan Centaur , the successor to the venerable Atlas V. Dream Chaser was supposed to ride on Vulcan's second-ever mission but wasn't ready in time, so that flight went ahead in October 2024 without the space plane. Sierra Space is now targeting spring 2027 for Dream Chaser's first liftoff, which will be a free-flying test mission in Earth orbit. The company is now pursuing many types of contracts for Dream Chaser, anticipating a mix of missions for NASA, the U.S. military and private companies — including the consortiums that plan to build commercial space stations. Indeed, Sierra Space is a member of one such consortium — the group that plans to build an outpost known as Orbital Reef .

item.title: A Magna Carta for the stars: King Charles III takes on space sustainability
item.description: null We live in the era of the satellite. They power our phones, banking infrastructure, navigational systems and internet, while providing stunning imagery and data that can be used to direct emergency services, feed weather forecasts and help coordinate military assets. But low-Earth orbit is not an infinite resource. It's starting to get crowded, with over 16,000 satellites and over 1.2 million pieces of debris currently circling our planet at incredible speeds. And if not managed properly, the results could be catastrophic. "In the early days of the space age actors could more or less ignore the other actors," Peter Martinez, executive director of the Secure World Foundation told Space.com. "You know the big sky paradigm, right? You can do what you want because the chances of your actions affecting others are minuscule." As noted by Martinez, the modern orbital landscape is radically different from those early frontier days, especially since the mid 2010s and the advent of satellite megaconstellations. "Nowadays, we really do have to worry about orbital congestion, and because space is out of sight for most people, we don't." Each new rocket launch leaves a footprint on the orbital environment, whether it be the satellite payloads they place in orbit or the pieces of inert hardware they leave behind such as an interstage adapter or rocket body. All of those objects create an ever-increasing risk of collisions. 130 million pieces of debris are currently estimated to be orbiting Earth. (Image credit: ESA) In a worst case scenario, clouds of debris spawned by colliding spacecraft could create a cascading effect known as the Kessler syndrome , with the potential to render the orbital environment completely unusable, trapping us on Earth . Enter King Charles III's Astra Carta, an all-encompassing roadmap to space exploration that launched on June 28, 2023 with a clear but ambitious mandate — to place sustainability at the core of humanity's presence beyond Earth. What is the Astra Carta? The Astra Carta stands as the space-focused sibling of the Terra Carta — a voluntary framework that launched in 2021 with the goal of safeguarding Earth's natural splendor by championing a transition to global sustainability practices and environmental responsibility. Both names were chosen to draw comparison with the Magna Carta, a royal charter that served as an early foundation for the English Legal system and modern day democracies . The principles enshrined in the Astra Carta have the potential to be similarly transformative if taken to heart. "I have long felt that protecting space that immediately surrounds our planet is one of those issues few recognize as important, but like so many of our present challenges, that were ignored for too long, if we do not address it quickly, it will come back to haunt us in a big way," the then-Prince of Wales stated in a message to participants of the 4th Summit for Space Sustainability in June 2022. item.title: NASA's interstellar Voyager 1 probe is about to reach 1 light-day from Earth after nearly 50 years in space
item.description: null Voyager 1 is celebrating a big milestone as it approaches its 50th birthday: reaching one light-day away from Earth. NASA's long-running interstellar Voyager 1 probe will mark one light-day of distance from Earth on Nov. 18, when the spacecraft is 49 years, two months and 11 days old. The agency recently stated the record distance, which will be reached at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (101607 GMT) is "a huge milestone by any measure, and a day worth celebrating." During the light-day crossover, Voyager will be in contact with the Madrid station of the three-antenna Deep Space Network that monitors all deep-space missions. The spacecraft is currently making its way through the constellation Ophiuchus from the perspective of Earth, said Jeffrey Hayes, a NASA official whose work includes Voyager 1. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) "This [milestone] essentially kicks off the year's worth of celebrations leading up to the 50th anniversary in August and September of next year," added Hayes, who is discipline scientist in the agency's astrophysics and heliophysics divisions, in a livestreamed discussion with NASA's Night Sky Network on Nov. 4. Going the distance Voyager 1 is the farthest spacecraft from Earth, after launching from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Sept. 5, 1977 a few weeks after its twin, Voyager 2 . NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft launches atop a Titan/Centaur-6 rocket from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Sept. 5, 1977. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/KSC) A light-day, as the name implies, represents the distance that light travels in a single day. In other words, at one light-day, a radio-wave message to Voyager 1 takes 24 hours to get to the spacecraft — which is roughly 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers) from Earth. Voyager's response then takes another day to get back to our planet. Voyager 2 — which is at a distance of 13.5 billion miles (21.7 billion km) from our planet — won't hit the light-day milestone until 2035, NASA stated. While the agency has not offered recent estimates for how long the two spacecraft will last, in 2022 Suzanne Dodd, project manager for Voyager at JPL, said they may keep operating into the 2030s . The two spacecraft had initial funding to survey Jupiter and Saturn, although NASA did launch them at a time when the planets aligned in such a way to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune if funding continued — which it did. Voyager 1, meanwhile, took a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings, and the pre-biotic (pre-life chemistry) moon of its largest moon Titan , executing maneuvers which brought it high above the solar system's plane. item.description: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 16 – NGC… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. NGC 7129: Star Formation with Jets from Webb Explanation: How do stars form? To help answer this question, NASA used the James Webb Space Telescope to take the featured detailed image of the star-forming region NGC 7129 in infrared light . Star formation progresses when gravity pulls together massive amounts of gas, but soon things can get complicated when previously formed stars emit powerful jets and winds — and some then explode . Opaque dust can form in the cool atmospheres of stars and, when dispersed, can obstruct visible-light images. Many stars can be seen to be forming in the featured image , with the young stars on the left, in the gold-colored gas, typically being more mature than the young stars on the right — in the red region. Jets and wind s likely cause the filamentary nature of the red-colored gas. Studying stars at different stages of development bolsters understanding about what physical processes are most important and when. item.description: null You just ordered a Pizza Hut and a two-liter bottle of Mountain Dew. You put on "Space Jam" to watch the greatest of all time team up with the Looney Tunes. It's a perfect evening… in 1996 or 2026. The entire concept of "Space Jam" is so '90s that you swear you can hear Los Del Rio in the background mouthing, "Dale a tu cuerpo alegría, Macarena." As ridiculous as an intergalactic basketball match may sound, it's a perfect example of how even the strangest idea can work if you commit to it fully. In case you thought you hallucinated the whole thing, no, you didn't, as the Looney Tunes find themselves in quite the predicament in this live-action-animation hybrid. A bunch of aliens known as the Nerdlucks arrive on Earth to abduct the Tunes and take them back as attractions to the outer-space amusement park known as Moron Mountain (shockingly nobody has claimed that subreddit, so do your thing, Internet!). Being a wheeling-and-dealing wabbit, though, Bugs Bunny proposes a winner-takes-all basketball game between the Tunes and the tiny Nerdlucks. Unfortunately, the crafty aliens use their tech to steal the talent from ballers like Charles Barkley and Muggsy Bogues and turn themselves into the scary and skilled Monstars. So, Bugs and friends reach out to Michael Jordan, who recently switched from basketball to baseball, to help the Tune Squad win this intergalactic b-ball matchup and their freedom, because if anybody can do it, Air Jordan (Hare Jordan?) can. Oh, Bill Murray also shows up here a few times. Why? Because he can! (Image credit: Warner Bros. Pictures) "Space Jam" is a spin on the classic sci-fi trope of resolving high-stakes conflicts through sports. In 1975, "Death Race 2000" introduced a world where people drive like hooligans and bash into each other to get ahead and win races (ironically, this is the regular experience on any public road now). Yet "Space Jam" took this concept, cartoonified it for a family-friendly audience, and challenged the conflict resolution approaches of other alien invasion movies from 1996. item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
item.description: null On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds. When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use. Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001. (Image credit: NRAO/AUI/NSF) Why it mattered When the 300-foot telescope first debuted, it was not just the United States' largest radio observatory, but the largest such facility in the world. But its quick construction — just two years — led to it having to be significantly upgraded later. "In 1970, the 300-foot’s surface had become so warped from maintenance crews, snow, and its own weight that a new finer-meshed aluminum surface was installed," the website for the National Radio Astronomy Observatory reads. "A larger traveling feed was also installed at the prime focus." The collapse, however, was no one's fault. "Unforeseeable stress factors cracked a steel connector plate," wrote the NRAO. The Green Bank Telescope collapse left a mass of twisted debris behind. (Image credit: NRAO/AUI/NSF) During its years of observations, the 300-foot telescope contirbuted to the discovery of dark matter and the realization that pulsars come from supernova explosions. "One of the most important products to come out of the 300-foot telescope was an all-sky survey of radio objects called the Green Bank 6cm Survey. Nearly every northern hemisphere radio object studied by any other telescope is from a catalog compiled using this telescope," reads the NRAO website. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

item.title: Why hasn't the 'Blaze Star' exploded yet? Astronomers weigh in on what to expect
item.description: null For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out. What is T. Coronae Borealis? T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold. Next comes a dramatic nova explosion that causes the star to flare to 1,000 times its usual brightness before gradually settling down and repeating the cycle. Why is it so challenging to predict T. CrB's nova flare? "T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon," Bradley Schaefer of the Louisiana State University Department of Physics and Astronomy told Space.com in an email. "Everyone is very confident on this. But we cannot make high-accuracy measures of the rate of gas falling onto the surface of the white dwarf, and we do not have a high accuracy measure of the trigger mass for the big hydrogen bomb." Schaefer continued. Historical observations reveal that the last nova eruption reached Earth in 1946, which places us well inside the window for another dramatic brightening of T. CrBb. However, the unpredictability of the white dwarf's feeding makes it difficult to pin down exactly when the explosion will become visible from Earth. An animation of T. CrB brightening. (Image credit: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab) "The exact date of the upcoming T CrB eruption depends primarily on how fast the gas coming from its companion star is accumulating on the surface of the white dwarf," explained Schaefer. "When some specific trigger mass has accumulated, then T CrB will erupt. For the last 80 years, we have been watching the gas pile up on the white dwarf surface, and we know that it must be near the trigger threshold." Astronomers have tried to predict T CrB's brightening by comparing a recent fluctuation in the light of the distant star system to a similar event that occurred in the runup to the 1946 event. "There have already been some dimming and brightening episodes that caused excitement but did not yet turn into the main event," Elizabeth Hays, lab chief at NASA's Astroparticle Physics Laboratory at the Goddard Spaceflight Center , told Space.com in an email. "It is likely that the nova will happen in the next few years but we still don't know exactly when. I can't give you a guaranteed prediction, but I will be a little surprised if it gets to 2030, or 84 years past the last eruption." item.description: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year. On June 14, as it headed towards perihelion – the closest point in its orbit to the sun, at a distance from our star of 1.5 times the distance between the Earth and the sun (known as an astronomical unit) , 220P suddenly and without warning burst into life. On 31 May, the comet was languishing at magnitude +17.39 (the higher the magnitude, the fainter an object is), but within less than 14 hours it had dramatically brightened to magnitude +11.05, bringing it into range for observation with small amateur telescopes. By June 2, 220P was up to magnitude +8.23 and was technically visible for a short while in 10x50 binoculars from a dark site, prompting amateur astronomers and astrophotographers to chase down this rare event. By perihelion, the comet had faded back to magnitude +12, but more was to come. A second outburst began at the end of July, brightening from magnitude +14 on 28 July to magnitude 6.1 by 6 August. Telling the tale of a dirty snowball Comets are often referred to as dirty snowballs, and beneath their dusty crust are ices made from various volatiles, including water, carbon dioxide and nitrogen. Solar heating, even at the distance of Mars, can cause these ices to rapidly sublimate into gases, and the pressure of the escaping gas rips the surface apart, spewing huge amounts of dust in to space. Models based on observations of 220P’s outburst indicate that it spewed out between tens of billions and hundreds of billions of pounds’ worth of cometary dust that filled the comet’s coma, the diffuse 'atmosphere' that clings to the comet’s solid nucleus. The dust particles, which are just millionths of a meter across, expanded outwards from the comet at about 1,280 feet (390 meters) per second, scattering sunlight and causing the coma to substantially brighten. "We have concluded that the comet detached localized parts of its crust, creating a dust-rich envelope that increased [the comet’s brightness by] 250 times in half a day," Josep M. Trigo-Rodríguez, of the Institut de Ciències de l’Espai and the Institute of Space Studies of Catalonia in Spain, said in a statement . item.title: What's next for SpaceX's Starship after epic Flight 15 chopsticks catch?
item.description: null Starship may have just made history, but it still has some work to do to get fully up and running. The megarocket launched on its 15th test flight on Friday (Nov. 13), aiming to pull off a dramatic and unprecedented twofer. SpaceX wanted to bring both Starship elements — its Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage — back to the launch pad at its Starbase site in Texas to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms. It didn't happen with Super Heavy; the booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday evening after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship came home successfully , nestling into the tower's arms in a soft and unprecedented embrace on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after lifting off. Long-distance view of Ship's historic landing on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) SpaceX has caught Super Heavy on three test flights to date. But it had never caught a Ship before; indeed, it had never even tried before Saturday. It's tougher and riskier to catch Ship; the upper stage flies much higher and faster than Super Heavy, so its return trip is much more more involved. Saturday was therefore a very big day for the company. "That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel," SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said during the company's landing webcast on Saturday. "We caught a Starship, and now everything changes." The F light 15 mission plan gave us a sneak peek at the future: The double catch will be standard on operational Starship missions, as this recovery strategy will enable rapid inspection, refurbishment and reflight of the megarocket, according to SpaceX. And the company is indeed planning on rapid reflight. Elon Musk has said that SpaceX is targeting 10,000 Starship launches per year by 2030, which works out to more than one liftoff every hour on average. Why such a mind-boggling cadence? Because SpaceX plans to build megaconstellations far larger than anything circling Earth today. For example, it wants its next-gen Starlink V3 broadband network to consist of 100,000 satellites . And its planned Starmind AI data-center constellation will be 10 times bigger than that, featuring one million spacecraft , if all goes to plan. For perspective: SpaceX's current-gen Starlink network in low Earth orbit (LEO), by far the largest constellation ever assembled, is about 11,000 strong at the moment. A look at the 33 Raptor engines of Starship's Super Heavy booster during the vehicle's Flight 15 test launch on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: Josh Dinner, Space.com/Future) Rocket recovery is only part of the reuse equation, of course; there's also refurbishment and reflight. And that gets us back to the "work left to do" discussion, for SpaceX has yet to demonstrate rapid reflight with either Super Heavy or Ship. When we think of extraterrestrials, our minds generally go from the latex-suited bipedal aliens seen in Star Trek and Star Wars to more exotic critters in sci-fi movies. Scientists think in terms of carbon-based microbial life and other lower life forms. item.title: 'Alien: Fireteam Elite 2' is a good old-fashioned bug hunt, ironically plagued by bugs
item.description: The first Aliens: Fireteam Elite was among my favorite Alien video games , and there were a lot of reasons to be excited for a sequel. At Summer Game Fest 2026 , we learned of many smart changes and improvements to the formula, and I was eager to go bug-hunting again. A new campaign, fully reworked classes, and four-player co-op. What could go wrong? Months later, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2's debut has been difficult, mostly due to glaring tech issues. Despite this, it's still a welcome jolt of action for a franchise that's been focusing on making the Xenomorphs scary again in recent years. Alien: Romulus (2024) and Alien: Earth (2025) have reestablished the acid-blooded Xenomorphs as bona fide horror icons, while games like Aliens: Dark Descent bet on tense real-time tactics and squad management; Rogue Incursion spooked VR and non-VR players alike; and we even have Isolation 2 's pure survival horror to look forward to. Rough edges aside, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 is a necessary return to mindless shooting and treating the Xenos as a relentless horde, dropping the stalking and slasher-inspired murders in favor of sci-fi shootouts and macho one-liners. It's far from a novel idea — even the original game is only five years old — but a classic for a reason. Another glorious day in the Corps (Image credit: Daybreak Game Company) Believe it or not, another colony has fallen prey to the Xenomorphs in Fireteam Elite 2. The familiar setup takes a new team of Colonial Marines to a mining facility on LV-558, where contact has been lost with the first wave of Marines that went in to deal with the threat. This isn't first contact; the Marines are more than used to bug hunts by now, which means there's less exposition to cut through before getting to the Xeno-blasting chaos. The writing certainly won't stun the Academy (and there's definitely too much of it in between missions), but the agility here is appreciated. We've fought these aliens many, many times before. Fireteam Elite 2 is smart enough to sidestep fake tension and just hit the ground running. (Image credit: Daybreak Game Company) All the design changes and upgrades reinforce the intent to make the ultimate Aliens action game. Classes have more defined roles and access to better, more destructive sci-fi weapons, and the upgrade to four-player fireteams is welcome when aliens and hostile synths won't stop pouring in. Tired of replaying campaign missions on higher difficulties and with modifiers? Prepare for the worst in this shooter's version of the classic horde mode. At its best, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 understands why James Cameron's masterpiece still holds up. During the biggest Xenomorph onslaughts — when the bullets are flying and acid is spraying — the game's shortcomings and jankier elements fade away. item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 14, 1969: NASA's Apollo 12 astronauts launch to the moon on a 'pinpoint landing' lunar mission
item.description: null On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 mission launched to the moon. This was the second moon landing of the Apollo program. The two astronauts on board were Pete Conrad , commander, and Alan Bean , the lunar module pilot. Astronaut Richard Gordon , the command module pilot, stayed in the command module and orbited the moon while his crewmates went to the surface. The astronauts made a pinpoint landing in a lunar mare called the Ocean of Storms. The previous moon mission, Apollo 11 , drifted far from the planned landing zone. But Apollo 12 landed close to a scientific target. That target was a robotic lander called Surveyor 3 . Scientists wanted to look at Surveyor 3 to see how well the spacecraft lasted on the moon since it landed there more than two years earlier. The Apollo 12 moonwalkers also performed a lot of moon science. The astronauts picked up 75 pounds of moon rocks. Most of the rocks were basalts that formed from molten lava. These basalts showed the Apollo 12 landing site is more than 3 billion years old. The Apollo 12 astronauts on NASA's second crewed moon landing mission. They are (left to right) are Charles Conrad Jr., Richard F. Gordon Jr., and Alan L. Bean. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered Apollo 12 proved that the Apollo 11 moon landing was not just a one-off stunt while setting the stage for even more ambitious missions. To truly explore the moon and advance our understanding of how our solar system formed, the follow-on Apollo flights needed to be able to land where the geologists had identified as areas of interest. Apollo 12, with its touchdown in proximity to the Surveyor probe, proved this was possible. The Apollo 12 astronauts visited NASA's Surveyor 3 lander and took samples of it back to Earth. (Image credit: NASA) The launch of Apollo 12 also underscored the importance of having a well-prepared Mission Control team, an asset that would be critical to outcome of the next mission, Apollo 13. The ability to recover from a complete electrical short out with the simple call of a through of a switch "SCE to AUX" proved that knowing every detail about how the spacecraft worked was key to a successful program. item.title: 'Now everything changes': SpaceX catches Starship upper stage for 1st time ever (video)
item.description: null SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), a landmark achievement that could unlock the giant vehicle's immense potential. Starship launched on its 15th test flight on Friday evening (Nov. 13), rising into the sky from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas. The mission plan called for bringing both of the vehicle's stages back to Starbase and catching them with the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — an unprecedented total recovery of an orbital rocket . That didn't happen; Starship's Super Heavy booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship succeeded in its attempt, notching a huge milestone for SpaceX and its dream of full rocket reuse. "That was the missing link," SpaceX's Dan Huot said during the company's landing webcast today, his voice thick with emotion. "That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel. We caught a Starship, and now everything changes." SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), a landmark achievement that could unlock the giant vehicle's immense potential. (Image credit: Josh Dinner/Space.com) The Ship catch occurred today at 4:20 p.m. EST (2120 GMT; 3:20 p.m. local Texas time), roughly 22.5 hours after Flight 15 lifted off. Many SpaceX employees went outside to watch the vehicle, known as Ship 42, descend through the clouds toward its Starbase launch tower, which the company calls "Mechazilla." And they got quite a show: Ship 42 nestled gently into Mechazilla's waiting arms, while "Baby Come Back" played over SpaceX's landing webcast. "This is so incredible to see," SpaceX's Jessie Anderson said during the livestream. "One of the most incredible and historic engineering feats of all time has just happened right in front of our eyes." Why was this such a big deal? SpaceX had already caught Super Heavy — on three previous Starship test flights, in fact. But it had never tried before with Ship. The upper stage is a tougher target, for it flies higher, farther and faster than the booster. Indeed, on Flight 15, Ship 42 came all the way back down from orbit. Ship 42 comes in for its landing on Nov. 14, 2026. item.title: See Jupiter and Mars make a spectacular close approach overnight Nov. 15-16
item.description: null Heads up stargazers! Mars meets Jupiter for a spectacular rendezvous in the heart of the constellation Leo on the night of Nov. 15-16, and they won't be this close again until July 2029. Jupiter and Mars will appear a little over 1 degree from each other as they rise over the eastern horizon around midnight for viewers in the U.S., as the blue-white light of the main-sequence star Regulus glows below, according to In-The-Sky . It's all a trick of perspective, but spectacular nonetheless. In reality Mars and Jupiter are separated by a gulf of over 368 million miles (592 million kilometers), while the light from Regulus has travelled for some 79 light-years before reaching Earth . The spectacular display occurs just once every 2-2.5 years , when Mars catches up to Jupiter as it plies its more distant orbit, making the pair appear side by side from our Earthly vantage point — an event known to astronomers as an appulse. Jupiter, Mars and Regulus will appear close together on the night of Nov. 15-16. (Image credit: Created by Anthony Wood in Canva.) Both Mars and Jupiter are "superior planets" whose orbits exist beyond that of Earth. As a result their disks always appear full to us through the eyepiece of a telescope, unlike the inner planets Mercury and Venus , which exhibit moon-like phases as they circle the sun . A 6-inch telescope can reveal the wildly differing natures of the solar system worlds. Slew your scope to Jupiter to spot the gargantuan cloud bands (and zones) that ring the gas giant , formed from masses of ammonia and water that travel in different directions through Jupiter's hydrogen and helium atmosphere, driven by powerful jet streams. How to measure distances in the night sky using your outstretched hand. (Image credit: Created in Canva Pro) Mars, meanwhile, appears as a reddish, ochre disk complete with dark surface features, where basaltic rock has been scoured clean of the iron-rich dust that covers much of its surface, according to NASA . item.title: New Scientist readers on how the magazine has shaped their lives
item.description: Have you been reading New Scientist since the start? Getty Images/Westend61 The first issue of New Scientist was published on 22 November 1956, and some of our readers have been with us since the very beginning. We asked subscribers, young and old, to tell us how they first encountered the magazine and how New Scientist has influenced their lives. The volume of responses and the gratitude expressed within them were quite overwhelming. Here are some of our favourites, featuring a spectacular maggot experiment, science-inspired poetry and even a match made on the short-lived New Scientist dating site. Huge thanks to everyone who wrote in. I was interested to see that New Scientist was launched “for all those men and women who are interested in scientific discovery and in its industrial, commercial and social consequences”. At the age of 13, I saved up a shilling from my Saturday morning “jobs” to purchase the first edition on 22 November 1956 and became one of those people interested in scientific discovery. Seventy years later, I remain a subscriber, after a scientific career that took me to many (if not, most!) countries in the world. New Scientist covered things like the opening of Jodrell Bank telescope in 1957. Since that was only about 50 miles (80 kilometres) away, it necessitated a bike ride to see what it really looked like! Peter Hall Advertisement I seem to have been reading New Scientist for the full 70! I do recall my encounter with the first edition: I was at Bec Grammar School in south London in a second-year physics class – it was 1956. The teacher, a genial boffin-type, announced the advent of the new publication and handed out copies – all I remember is its grey (or was it beige?) pages, which I read in a perfunctory way (I was only 12!) little thinking it would follow me through life and around the globe. Robyn Williams I was at Malvern College in England for my O level examinations from 1955 to 1958. My science master at Malvern had recognised my interest in science and technology and he bought the very first issue of New Scientist with his own money. At the next science class, he stood up in front of the whole class and waved the first issue, saying, “Young Inman, a new UK science and technology magazine has been published and here is the first issue for you.” I went on to reach 60 years as a member of the UK Institution of Civil Engineers. Peter Inman 1956 puts me back at school – Fettes College in Edinburgh. The school adopted New Scientist from its first edition and it was available in the library, where senior boys interested in science were recommended to read it. And so began a lifetime of New Scientist – I have been a regular for as long as I can remember and a subscriber for a very long time. I am very grateful to New Scientist for maintaining my interest in all the sciences and new developments, which I am sure has helped me to think laterally and to have a greater understanding of what makes everything tick. item.title: SpaceX launches Starship on ambitious 22-hour Flight 15 test, but aborts booster 'chopsticks' catch (video)
item.description: null STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX launched the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket today (Nov. 13) and is preparing the vehicle's upper stage for its first-ever return to the launch site in less than 24 hours. Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX 's Starbase facility here in South Texas at 5:47 p.m. ET (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local Texas time). The towering Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage cleared the tower without incident and climbed into the skies under more than 18 million pounds of thrust from the booster's 33 Raptor 3 engines. The flight continued nominally through its initial ascent, with the successful execution of Super Heavy's main engine cutoff and Ship's subsequent hot-staging — firing its own Raptors during separation from the booster — about 2.5 minutes after launch. Following stage separation, Super Heavy reoriented for a planned return to Starbase as Ship powered its way toward low Earth orbit (LEO). SpaceX originally planned to catch Super Heavy with the Starbase launch tower's giant mechanical "chopstick" arms. But it wasn't to be: The company called off the catch attempt and brought the booster down for a controlled splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico about 6.5 minutes after launch, for reasons that were not immediately clear. A successful catch would have been a significant milestone for SpaceX and its efforts to design Starship as a fully and rapidly reusable launch vehicle. It would have been the first successful recovery of a Version 3 (V3) Super Heavy , which SpaceX began flying earlier this year. The company previously recovered three of its V1 Super Heavy vehicles and reused two of those in later flights. SpaceX's Starship megarocket launches on its 15th test flight from Starbase, Texas on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Future/Josh Dinner, Space.com) Ship goes to orbit Ship's Raptors continued to fire following stage separation, completing their first burn just after eight minutes into flight. All went according to plan after that for Ship as well: A second engine burn lasting about 20 seconds parked Ship in LEO at an altitude of around 170 miles (275 kilometers) at T+26 minutes and 10 seconds. "We’ve got a nominal orbit insertion, so Starship now in orbit around Earth for the second time ever," SpaceX's Dan Huot said during today's Flight 15 launch webcast. "That’s a really great moment." Ship first reached orbit on Flight 14 , which launched on Sept. 28. Ship carried 26 of SpaceX's Starlink V3 spacecraft, which were deployed into LEO on schedule today over a 42-minute span starting 35 minutes after launch. The upgraded wireless internet satellites are the second V3 batch to reach orbit, after a set of 26 that were delivered on Flight 14 . V3s are significantly more powerful than SpaceX's V2 Starlinks, which currently number more than 11,000 in LEO. item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 13, 1971: NASA's Mariner 9 becomes 1st spacecraft to orbit Mars, revealing close looks at the Martian surface
item.description: null On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. At the time, scientists didn't know much about the Red Planet. NASA had several Mars flybys before Mariner 9 . Those flybys showed that Mars had a cratered surface , so some scientists thought that Mars looked just like the moon. Then Mariner 9 blew blew their minds. When Mariner 9 got to Mars , it arrived in the middle of a dust storm. It saw some tall structures sticking through the clouds. When the dust settled, images from Mariner 9 revealed that these structures were the tops of huge volcanoes. One volcano, Olympus Mons , is the tallest in the solar system. Mariner 9 also spotted an enormous canyon called Valles Marineris . This canyon is five times longer than the Grand Canyon in Arizona. Mariner 9 worked for one year in orbit. When it ran out of gas, NASA shut it off. But the spacecraft remains one of the most famous Mars voyagers of all time. The Mariner 9 spacecraft, seen here in a NASA model, was the first to orbit Mars in 1971. (Image credit: NASA) Here's why it mattered Mariner 9 cemented its place in space history when it entered into orbit around Mars, the first human-built spacecraft ever to do so. The NASA spacecraft actually beat the Soviet Union's own Mars 2 spacecraft to the Red Planet, even though Mars 2 "had an 11-day head start," NASA said in a mission description . (Mars 2 would go on to be the first human-built craft to impact the surface of Mars when it crashed into the Red Planet.) But it was the science from Mariner 9 that transformed Mars from a mysterious Red Planet into a full world for humans to explore. The Boldest Mars Missions in History The Mariner 9 mission first saw the peak of Olympus Mons on Mars in the midst of a global dust storm in 1971. (Image credit: NASA/JPL) Mariner 9 carried four primary instruments to study Mars, including a camera system for imaging, an ultraviolet spectrometer, an infrared spectrometer and an infrared radiometer. The probe mapped 85% of Mars with those tools during its nearly one-year mission. The Mariner 9 spacecraft discovered 20 giant volcanoes on Mars (including Olympus Mars) and made key observations to map Valles Marineris, which runs 2,500 miles (4,000 kilometers) long acros the Tharsis region and is 120 miles (200 km) wide. "The canyon was named in honor of Mariner 9," NASA said in an overview . In all, Mariner 9 took 7,329 photos of the surface of Mars, mapping the planet down to a resolution of between 1/2-1 mile (1-2 km). It also snapped at least 80 photos of Phobos and Deimos, the two small moons of Mars. By February 1972, Mariner 9's supply of gaseous nitrogen, which it used to feed its attitide control thrusters, had run dry. NASA finally shut down the mission in October 1972. item.title: 60 years ago the Leonid meteor shower produced 144,000 meteors per hour. Could it happen again?
item.description: null This year marks a rather auspicious anniversary for meteor watchers. Sixty years ago , one of the most stupendous Leonid meteor displays lit up the predawn skies over the central and western U.S. So, what will the 2026 Leonids bring us? And what might they bring in the years to come? The Leonid meteor shower is one of the most celebrated of the year's annual displays of "shooting stars." The mere mention of the Leonids usually elicits mental images of a sky filled with shooting stars pouring down through the sky like rain. Such meteor storms have indeed occurred with the Leonids, such as in 1833 and 1966 when meteor rates of tens of thousands per hour were observed. In more recent years, most notably 1999 , 2001 and 2002 , lesser Leonid displays of up to "only" a few thousand meteors per hour took place. Unfortunately, that's not likely to be the case this year. In fact, comparatively speaking, this is going to be a lean year for the Leonids chiefly because of the expected lack of any significant activity. Although the Leonids are one of the most famous of all the annual meteor displays, this year they're not likely to be very productive. It's probable they are going to be rather weak and there probably will be long stretches when not a single Leonid will be seen. I'll explain why in a moment. First, let's find out about this shower's lineage. What causes the Leonids? The Leonids are so named because the shower's radiant point, from where the meteors seem to fan out, is located within the constellation of Leo the Lion, from the backward question mark pattern of stars known as " The Sickle." The meteors are caused by the Tempel-Tuttle comet , which sweeps through the inner solar system every 33⅓ years. Each time the comet passes closest to the sun it leaves a "river of rubble" in its wake: a dense trail of dusty debris. A meteor storm becomes possible if the Earth were to score a direct hit on a fresh dust trail ejected by the comet over the past several centuries. The "lion's share" (no pun intended) of comet dust can be found just ahead and trailing behind Tempel-Tuttle. That comet last swept through the inner solar system in 1998. That's why spectacular meteor showers were seen in 1999, 2001 and 2002, with declining numbers thereafter. The most famous depiction of the 1833 Leonids, actually produced in 1888 for the Adventist book Bible Readings for the Home Circle .
